claims.text: In predominantly BCC refractory high-entropy alloys, strength is governed by the prevalence of edge dislocations.
In predominantly BCC refractory high-entropy alloys, hardness is governed by the prevalence of edge dislocations.
Edge dislocations undergo thermally activated super-jogging.
Thermal super-jogging creates robust barriers to further dislocation motion.
The barriers created by edge-dislocation super-jogging produce an elevated-temperature yield-strength plateau.
NbTaTiZrV0.5 is a single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy suitable as the initial state.
NbTaTiZrV0.5 has documented chemical inhomogeneity and lattice distortions.
Local lattice distortions enhance the thermal super-jogging of edge dislocations.
At lower temperatures, dislocation motion is limited by intrinsic lattice resistance.
Increasing temperature generally makes dislocation motion easier and causes strength to decline.
Plastic flow in pure and dilute BCC alloys is typically controlled by thermally activated screw-dislocation motion.
Thermal super-jogging of edge dislocations dynamically counteracts ordinary high-temperature softening.
Alloys dominated by screw dislocations show a continuous decrease in yield strength with temperature.
An edge-dislocation-rich NbTaTiZrV0.5-like HEA should show an approximately temperature-independent yield-strength plateau from roughly 673 K to 1073 K.
Edge dislocations should be prevalent and dominant during the high-temperature strength plateau.
The proposed mechanism is limited to predominantly BCC HEAs with substantial chemical inhomogeneity that promotes edge-dislocation formation.
The mechanism may not apply to FCC or HCP HEAs or to alloys whose primary plasticity mechanism is nanotwinning.
Failure to observe either the 673–1073 K yield-strength plateau or prevalent edge dislocations would falsify edge-dislocation super-jogging as the primary strength-retention mechanism.

contradictions.description: The prediction requires edge dislocations to be prevalent during the plateau but does not predict a temperature-induced change in dislocation type. The falsification rule nevertheless treats observing no change in dislocation type as falsifying, even if edge dislocations remain dominant throughout.
